questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a research proposal is for
questions.learningObjective: state what a proposal must let a reader decide
questions.stem: A research proposal is required before a project may begin. What must the proposal let a reader do?

options.text: Decide whether the project is worth doing and whether it can be done, since a proposal is judged on both and a section answering one cannot supply the other
See what the researcher already knows, since the existing work is the main thing a proposal exists to display to those judging it
options.misconception: makes the proposal a demonstration of the author's learning rather than a case for a project

options.text: Check the conclusions in advance, since a reader who can anticipate the findings will judge them more fairly than one who cannot
options.misconception: asks a proposal to deliver its own results, which is a reason a proposal is written before the work rather than after

options.text: Follow the plan step by step, since a detailed schedule is the part of a proposal that carries the most weight with those approving it
options.misconception: makes the schedule the substance of a proposal, and leaves the question and the design unjudgeable

questions.explanation: A proposal is an argument that a particular project should happen, and arguments have two audiences of objection. One member of the panel thinks the question is not worth answering, and the other thinks the design will not answer it. A proposal that answers only the first is a statement of interest; a proposal that answers only the second is a piece of technical work in search of a purpose. The other options each reduce the document to one of its parts, and each of those parts is judged against the whole rather than for itself. A candidate who cannot say in a sentence what would be known afterwards has not yet written the first section.
questions.hint: Ask what two different objections the panel might raise that a proposal has to head off.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: How a contribution differs from a topic
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a proposed contribution from a subject area
questions.stem: A proposal's stated topic is how people in one city choose where to eat. What would make a contribution from that topic rather than the topic itself?

options.text: A claim about what the project would leave known that the existing work does not already leave known, since a topic names a subject and a contribution names a finding
A hypothesis stated in advance, since naming a proposition to be tested turns a subject into something a project can be said to have addressed
options.misconception: treats a testable proposition as the contribution, while a hypothesis is what the design tests rather than what it establishes

options.text: A method not previously used in that city, since applying a new instrument to a familiar question produces knowledge the old ones could not reach
options.misconception: makes novelty of method the contribution, which is a way of being new rather than a claim about what will be learned

options.text: A larger sample than earlier studies used, since a bigger body of evidence supports conclusions the smaller studies could only hint at
options.misconception: substitutes size for novelty of finding, and a larger sample narrows uncertainty without adding a question

questions.explanation: A topic is a region of enquiry and a contribution is a result, and the difference is what makes a proposal judgeable. A reader who can state the contribution can then ask whether it is right, whether it matters, and whether someone else has already produced it. A reader given only a topic has to supply the contribution themselves, and will supply whatever their priors suggest, which is not a basis on which to fund anything. The second option is a genuine step in writing a proposal, since a hypothesis does convert a subject into something to be tested, but the hypothesis is an input to the design rather than a claim about knowledge. Options three and four are the two most common substitutes, and both produce work that is competently done and unremarkable.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could say afterwards that they could not say before, and whether the topic statement does that.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Scope and the overreach risk
questions.learningObjective: identify the cost of proposing breadth a project cannot examine
questions.stem: A proposal sets out to study one national policy across fifty years and every sector it touched. What is the chief overreach risk in that scope?

options.text: That no part of it can be examined closely enough to bear a conclusion, since the attention available is fixed and breadth spends it on every part at once
That the necessary data will not exist, since a national record over fifty years is unlikely to have been kept in a single consistent form
options.misconception: supplies a practical difficulty the proposal could reduce by narrowing its period or sectors

options.text: That other researchers will object, since a project this broad belongs to several literatures and each of them will want it narrower
options.misconception: makes the main risk the reception, and treats what colleagues prefer as a measure of what will be found

options.text: That the results will be impossible to publish, since a project crossing sectors does not fit the pages any one journal accepts
options.misconception: concentrates on where the work could appear rather than on whether the scope can support a claim

questions.explanation: Breadth and depth spend the same budget, and the overreach risk is that a project claims conclusions about everything while having examined nothing in enough detail to support them. Fifty years across every sector means the design has to specify what counts as an instance in each, and the specification is where the study actually happens. A reader who suspects the candidate has not done that work is right to be suspicious. The other three options are real practical problems and each is survivable: data can be narrowed, colleagues can be engaged, and outlets can be found. They are also all downstream of the scope decision, which is why they are the wrong thing to be worried about first.
questions.hint: Ask what the project would have to do with a single year, and whether the design says.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Specificity of a methods section
questions.learningObjective: identify what a methods section must give beyond a list of stages
questions.stem: A proposal's methods section says data will be collected, analysed, and used to test the hypothesis. What does a section written that way fail to give?

options.text: The particulars another researcher would need in order to repeat the work, since naming the stages says what happens and not how any of it is done
A sample size, since no analysis can be regarded as credible until the number of observations has been fixed
options.misconception: names one missing particular and treats it as the whole, when a section can be unspecific about a dozen things

options.text: The name of the instrument, since measurements have to come from an established tool if the results are to be trusted by others
options.misconception: assumes a single standard instrument is required, while many projects build or adapt their own and say so

options.text: A schedule, since a method described without dates leaves the reader unable to judge whether the work fits the time available
options.misconception: puts the schedule inside the methods, and leaves the specificity question about the method itself unanswered

questions.explanation: A list of stages is a table of contents for a study. It tells a reader the shape of the work and nothing about the work, and it can be written before the researcher has decided anything difficult, which is why it appears in weak proposals. A methods section earns its place when somebody else could take it and do the project, which means specifying what was measured and how, who was included and how they were selected, what was done to the data, and what decisions were made where there was discretion. Options two and three are commonly missing particulars, and pointing at either as the single omission is a mistake because the sections that matter are unspecific throughout.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could carry out the study from this section without asking the researcher anything.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The dependency risk a timeline hides
questions.learningObjective: identify what a schedule leaves unstated when it lists dates without dependencies
questions.stem: A proposal's timeline gives each task a start and a finish date but never says which tasks depend on which. What risk does that leave hidden?

options.text: That a task will be scheduled as though it could start before what it needs exists, so one slip turns into a failure instead of a delay
That the total duration has been underestimated, since any list of tasks that omits the dependencies will also understate how long the work takes
options.misconception: states a consequence of the omission without naming what the schedule is failing to represent

options.text: That the researcher will not know what to do next, since a list without ordering gives no guidance about the sequence of the work
options.misconception: reads the dates as unusable, while a dated list still tells a reader when each task was meant to happen

options.text: That progress cannot be checked, since dates without dependencies make a slippage invisible until the end of the project
options.misconception: reframes the omission as a monitoring problem rather than a statement about the plan

questions.explanation: A list of dates is a set of assertions about when things will happen and not a statement of what has to happen first, and the difference only becomes visible the first time something runs late. A schedule that names no dependencies treats a delayed instrument as though the collection could go ahead, so the delay does not shift the work, it breaks it. The second option is close and worth being careful with, since a schedule that ignores dependencies usually does underestimate, but the reason is that the chain is invisible rather than that the arithmetic is wrong. Reviewers who ask for a schedule should ask what each task is waiting for, and that question is the one this proposal cannot answer.
questions.hint: Ask what each task is waiting for, and whether the schedule says.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The assumption a feasibility claim rests on
questions.learningObjective: identify what a claim of feasibility is predicting
questions.stem: A proposal is called feasible because the researcher has the time, the skills, and the access. What does that claim rest on?

options.text: That the access will hold at the scale assumed, since permission granted to a proposal is granted by someone who can withdraw it at any point
That the question is worth answering, since a project nobody would want the answer to is not worth doing well or otherwise
options.misconception: makes worth a matter of feasibility, and the two are the two separate questions a proposal is judged on

options.text: That the method has been used before, since a method nobody has tried cannot be costed in anyone's time
options.misconception: requires prior use of the method, when a feasible design may be new and still be within reach

options.text: That the budget is realistic, since feasibility is largely an accounting question about staff, materials, and money
options.misconception: reduces feasibility to cost, and leaves out access and timing which no budget can secure

questions.explanation: A feasibility claim is a prediction, and every prediction rests on something staying as it is. Here most of what the researcher controls is already settled, because their own time and skills are not in question. Access is the exception, and it is the part a proposal cannot guarantee: the institution, the archive, or the participants all have their own reasons, and any of them can change. That is the assumption a reviewer should press, and it is the one a candidate can usually say more about than they expect, since a specific account of who grants access and on what terms is worth more than a general assurance that access has been agreed.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three things the researcher can promise and which only someone else can promise.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The empty version of a significance claim
questions.learningObjective: identify what a significance claim must add beyond naming an important subject
questions.stem: A proposal claims its project is significant because it addresses an important topic that has so far been little studied. What is wrong with the claim as it stands?

options.text: It names a subject and a thin literature without saying what would be known afterwards, and a subject that is important is still not a contribution
It understates the project, since a topic studied little is often studied little for reasons that a new study would be wise to examine
options.misconception: treats the modesty as an error rather than as a claim that still lacks a stated result

options.text: It argues from the number of studies rather than their content, which is a problem with how the literature was counted rather than with the claim itself
options.misconception: locates the fault in a counting practice the claim does not describe

options.text: It is too modest for the field, since a claim of significance ought to promise a large effect rather than a modest finding
options.misconception: treats size of effect as the measure of significance, and rewards the grander claim regardless of what it would show

questions.explanation: This is the commonest weakness in a first proposal and it is easy to repair. The claim moves from the importance of a subject to the value of the project without an intermediate step, and the missing step is a claim about knowledge. Importance is a property the subject already has, whether or not this project happens, so citing it transfers nothing to the project. What a panel needs is the sentence a reader could repeat afterwards: this project will show that such and such is the case, and at present nobody knows whether it is. That sentence can then be judged, and it can turn out to be already established by work the candidate has not found, which is the next thing to look at.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would know after the project that they do not know now, and whether the claim says it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Verifying that a literature gap exists
questions.learningObjective: state how a claim that no prior work exists should be treated
questions.stem: A candidate claims that no previous work addresses the question their project will ask. How should that claim be treated?

options.text: As a claim to be checked, since a gap is an absence and an absence is not visible in any single search however wide that search is
As established, since a candidate who has read widely is the best available judge of what has and has not been done in a field
options.misconception: accepts a self-assessment as the check, and so makes the claim unfalsifiable for anyone else to test

options.text: As a strength, since a question nobody has asked guarantees there is room for a contribution and removes the risk of duplicating work
options.misconception: treats a gap as automatically good, and so stops asking whether the gap is real

options.text: As a reason to narrow the question, since a question nobody has asked is usually one too broad for a single project to address
options.misconception: draws a conclusion about scope from a claim about the literature, which is a separate question

questions.explanation: A gap is the one thing in a proposal that cannot be shown by exhibiting it, because what is being claimed is that nothing is there. The candidate's own confidence is the weakest possible evidence for it, since the candidate is the person with the most to gain and no way of seeing their own vocabulary. What helps is making the search inspectable: which sources, which terms, which years, and which neighbouring fields, so that somebody else can see where the search was thin and re-run it. It is also worth remembering that a verified gap is a weaker asset than candidates hope, since a question nobody has asked is sometimes a question nobody could answer with the data available.
questions.hint: Ask how somebody else could look for the same absence and get a different result.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A literature gap that is a search error
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a claimed gap as an artefact of how the search was run
questions.stem: A candidate searches one database using one set of terms and reports no prior study of a much-worked-on question. What is the likeliest explanation?

options.text: The terms followed the candidate's own way of describing the question, so work filed under different words was never brought into the results
The question really is untouched, since one database and a set of terms is a reasonable sample of what a field has produced
options.misconception: accepts one search as sufficient, and treats a large absence in one place as an absence everywhere

options.text: The work exists but is unpublished, since a question with nothing published about it must be one still in progress
options.misconception: invents an explanation about publication status that the search result gives no sign of

options.text: The database is itself incomplete, since no single database can be expected to hold the whole output of any field
options.misconception: blames the source for a defect in how it was queried, and so leaves the real cause untouched

questions.explanation: The failure here is almost always in the vocabulary rather than in the archive. A candidate who has a phrase for their question will search that phrase, and a literature that has approached the same problem from another discipline will have written about it in that discipline's terms, filed under a different heading and never retrieved. The repair is unglamorous: take the terms the candidate's own review found, and then take the terms used by the authors whose work the candidate found most similar, and search those as well. Candidates are often surprised by how much appears, and the useful lesson is that the first result of a search is information about the search.
questions.hint: Ask what words the nearest existing work would have used for the same problem.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The data requirement a research question imposes
questions.learningObjective: identify the respondents a question requires and the consequences of choosing others
questions.stem: A research question asks what members of a profession think a proposed standard should require. What data requirement does the question impose?

options.text: That the study reach members with formed views on the standard, since someone who has never encountered it cannot hold a view about what it should require
That the study be large, since views within a profession vary widely and only a big sample will show the variation rather than a few voices
options.misconception: substitutes size for the right kind of respondent, and a large sample of the wrong people is still the wrong people

options.text: That the study be anonymous, since members of one profession know one another and will answer differently if colleagues can identify them
options.misconception: raises a real design concern while leaving the question of who should be asked entirely unaddressed

options.text: That the study run for some time, since views about a standard change as the standard is used and a snapshot will miss that
options.misconception: assumes the standard is already in use, when the question is about one that is proposed

questions.explanation: A research question restricts who can answer it, and the restriction is easy to lose in a proposal that is written around the population a researcher can reach. Members who have used a standard have something to be for and against, and their answers are about requirements. Members who have never seen it will answer about something else, usually whether the proposal seems reasonable in the abstract, and the study will report that as though it were a view. The temptation is strong because the reachable population is usually the one the researcher already has, and recruiting the rest takes money and time. The other options are all defensible design considerations and none of them is the requirement the question itself imposes.
questions.hint: Ask what a member who has never seen the standard would be answering when asked what it should require.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A parameter the data cannot identify
questions.learningObjective: explain why a design fails when the target varies with something unmeasured
questions.stem: A project proposes to estimate how much of a difference in pay is due to a training programme, using workers' own reports of how much training they received. What is the problem?

options.text: The amount of training a worker reports may vary with something else that also moves pay, so the two cannot be told apart from these data however many are collected
The reports may be wrong, since people routinely misremember how much training they took and in what order
options.misconception: raises measurement error, which a larger sample reduces, and mistakes it for a problem of the design

options.text: The reports cannot be gathered at all, since pay records and training histories are generally held by different organisations
options.misconception: reports an obstacle to collection that a feasible study would simply have to plan around

options.text: The reports will not vary enough, since workers in a single workplace tend to have received much the same training
options.misconception: assumes the problem is too little variation rather than variation that travels with something else

questions.explanation: This is a failure of identification, and no amount of data will fix it. The project wants the part of a pay difference caused by the training, and it proposes to use the reported training as the thing that varies. If the people who report more training are also the people who were already more likely to be paid more, for any reason at all, then the two explanations of the pattern are indistinguishable in the data and each additional worker adds precision to an estimate of the wrong quantity. The fix is a design feature, not a sample size: something that varies the training independently of everything that moves pay, or a comparison the workers sort themselves into on grounds connected to pay. Option four describes a different problem and the opposite remedy.
questions.hint: Ask what else might separate the people who report more training from the people who report less.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The evidence chain a thesis requires
questions.learningObjective: identify what has to be evidenced separately in a causal thesis
questions.stem: A thesis claims that a policy reduced inequality. What has to be true for the evidence presented to support it?

options.text: That every link between the policy and the outcome is evidenced on its own, since a chain of reasoning is only as strong as its weakest joint
That the policy was large enough to have had an effect, since a small change is not going to move a measured outcome at all
options.misconception: sets a size condition on the cause, which is a power question rather than a question of the evidence

options.text: That the outcome was measured beforehand as well as afterwards, since a single measurement shows where a thing stands and not where it has moved to
options.misconception: names one design feature of one kind of study and treats it as the whole of what supporting a causal claim requires

options.text: That the affected group was comparable with an unaffected one, since comparison between groups is the whole basis on which a causal claim is made
options.misconception: assumes a comparison is the only route to a causal claim, and leaves open designs that identify the effect another way

questions.explanation: A thesis of this kind is a chain: the policy was implemented as intended, the implementation reached the people in question, the outcome was measured in a way that would register a change, and the change coincided with the policy rather than with everything else happening at the time. Each of those is a separate empirical claim, and a project that evidences one and asserts the other three has produced a conclusion with a single link. The other options each pick out a real design requirement and present it as the sufficient one, which is the characteristic failure of weak work: an adequate comparison, or a pre-measurement, does not by itself exclude every rival explanation for the pattern the researcher found.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would have to take on trust in order to believe the conclusion.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A thesis with a missing mechanism
questions.learningObjective: identify the unevidenced link between a finding and the explanation offered for it
questions.stem: A study finds that groups given a written agenda produced more proposals, and concludes that the agenda improved deliberation. What does that conclusion leave out?

options.text: A route from having an agenda to deliberating better, since the finding is equally consistent with an agenda simply prompting more people to speak at all
A larger sample, since a difference in counts of proposals is a small difference to be confident about
options.misconception: answers a question about precision, while the problem is which of two explanations of the same count the study can distinguish

options.text: A second kind of group, since only one sort of team was tested and the conclusion is offered about groups in general
options.misconception: raises a fair point about generalisation and presents it as though it were the missing piece in the explanation

options.text: A measure of deliberation, since the study counted proposals and nothing in the design assessed the thing the conclusion is about
options.misconception: proposes a different measure rather than noticing that the measure chosen does not bear on the claim made

questions.explanation: A mechanism is the story of how a cause produces an effect, and a finding is compatible with every mechanism that could produce it. More proposals could mean better deliberation, and it could equally mean that people who would have stayed silent were prompted to speak, which is a change in the count and not in the thinking. Nothing in the design tells the two apart, so the conclusion has skipped a link that has to be evidenced rather than assumed. The fourth option notices something true, that deliberation was not measured, and the honest version of it is the third answer: the measure is the count, the claim is about the thinking, and the project would have had to do something about the difference.
questions.hint: Ask what else an increase in the number of proposals could mean, and whether the design can tell the explanations apart.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a chapter in a long work is for
questions.learningObjective: state the function each chapter must perform in a long argument
questions.stem: A long piece of work is divided into chapters. What should each chapter be for?

options.text: To advance one step of the argument, so that the work reads as a sequence of steps rather than a pile of sections on a theme
To treat one source at length, since a chapter for each source keeps the reading of them and the writing about them separable
options.misconception: makes the sources the units, which produces a set of commentaries rather than an argument

options.text: To be of roughly standard length, since a reader working through a long work needs a predictable shape to navigate by
options.misconception: supplies a reason for equal chapters that has nothing to do with what a chapter is doing in the argument

options.text: To stand on its own, since a reader who opens a work at random should find a self-contained piece of argument in the chapter
options.misconception: asks each chapter to be independent, which removes the dependence between steps that makes a sequence an argument

questions.explanation: A chapter in a long work is a step, and a step exists because the next one needs it. Deciding what each chapter will argue is the most useful structural question a writer can ask, because it forces the question of order: which claim has to be in place before this evidence will mean anything, and which chapter will be unreadable if the reader has not yet got there. The second option is the arrangement that produces the least coherent kind of work, since a chapter per source makes the sources the structure and leaves the argument to be reassembled by the reader. The fourth is worth resisting explicitly, because self-contained chapters are pleasant to write and impossible to sequence.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader must already have understood before one chapter makes sense.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Chapter length and the one-argument constraint
questions.learningObjective: explain how a one-argument rule determines a chapter's length
questions.stem: A project's guidance says a chapter should contain a single argument. What does that rule do to the length of a chapter?

options.text: It makes the length a consequence of the argument, since some arguments take a page to state and others need sixty pages to establish
It fixes the length at whatever the guidance says, since the argument then has to be cut down or padded out to fit the space allowed
options.misconception: inverts the constraint, and treats a page allowance as the thing the argument must be fitted to

options.text: It makes chapters short, since one argument is by definition a small thing and a long chapter must be carrying more than one
options.misconception: assumes a single argument is a short one, when the rule constrains the number and not the size

options.text: It settles nothing about length, since a chapter's size is fixed by how much space the material needs and not by the guidance at all
options.misconception: denies the rule any structural effect, and leaves the writer with only a rule about count

questions.explanation: The rule is a rule about count, and count is what determines length in practice, because an argument does not stop being one argument at a page and does not become two at forty. A chapter that has a single claim to establish takes as long as establishing that claim properly takes, which may be short if the claim is obvious and long if it needs a great deal of the reader's attention paid to rival explanations. The value of the rule shows up in diagnosis rather than in length: a chapter that has run to sixty pages is a sign that three arguments are in there, and a chapter that ends after a page is a sign that the argument was not there. Option three mistakes the constraint, and option four throws away the only useful thing about it.
questions.hint: Ask how many separate claims to establish a chapter of sixty pages would contain.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an introduction has to do about existing work
questions.learningObjective: state what an introduction must establish about the literature
questions.stem: What must an introduction do about the existing work for a reader to be able to follow the project?

options.text: Say what the existing work has not established, since the project's own question only takes shape against something it is answering
Summarise the existing work, since a reader cannot understand what is new without knowing what was already there
options.misconception: describes a real requirement of an introduction and stops short of the one that carries the project

options.text: Cite the most recent work in the area, since a project is judged in part on whether its author knows the current state of the field
options.misconception: makes recency the requirement, which can be satisfied by a citation list that establishes nothing

options.text: Set out how earlier researchers approached the same question, since a reader wants to know what designs already exist before judging a new one
options.misconception: asks for a review of methods, which is useful background and does not establish what is missing

questions.explanation: The job of the introduction's review is not to inform but to position, and the thing it must position against is a specific limitation. A reader who has been shown that the existing work settles four things and leaves a fifth open understands the project immediately, and a reader who has been shown a summary of the field in general does not. This is also where a weak introduction is usually caught, since a vague review conceals the possibility that the gap does not exist, while a specific one invites a reviewer to check it. The second option is the most common failure to avoid, and the difficulty is that summarising the field feels like the work of an introduction and is not.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader would be able to conclude is still open after reading the section.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a methods chapter permit replication
questions.learningObjective: state the test a methods chapter must pass
questions.stem: What makes a methods chapter permit replication of the work it describes?

options.text: A reader could carry the study out again from what is written, since a method is specified when the steps and the materials are all given
The chapter is long enough to cover everything, since a short account will always have left some decision out and a long one has a better chance
options.misconception: confuses length with completeness, and a padded methods chapter omits as much as a brief one

options.text: The chapter uses the field's standard terminology, since terminology is what lets another researcher recognise a method they already know
options.misconception: makes shared vocabulary sufficient for reproducibility, when terms can be used loosely and still sound precise

options.text: The chapter reports what went wrong, since a reader who intends to repeat the work needs to know the difficulties to expect
options.misconception: values candour about difficulties over a specification that would let the work be done at all

questions.explanation: Replication is a practical test and it can be applied directly to a chapter: could somebody with access to the same materials carry this out and get something comparable? A chapter that passes has told its reader what was measured, on whom, how, what was recorded at each step, and what choices the researcher made where there was discretion. Where it fails, the reason is almost always a decision that has been described by its name rather than by its content, and those are the sentences a methods editor reads first. Options three and four are both real qualities of a good chapter and neither is the test, since recognisable terminology describes nothing and candour about difficulties is worth little to a reader who cannot tell what was done.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could do the work without asking the researcher a question.

questions.topic: Reporting in a results chapter
questions.learningObjective: distinguish reporting of findings from interpretation of them
questions.stem: What distinguishes a results chapter that reports from one that argues?

options.text: Whether the reading of the findings has been kept out of the report of them, so a reader can see what was found before being told what it means
Whether the chapter is written in the past tense, since tense is what separates what happened from what was meant by it
options.misconception: rests a substantive division on a grammatical one, and a tense convention is not a boundary on interpretation

options.text: Whether the data are presented as tables and figures, since data presented in raw form argue their point less effectively than data displayed
options.misconception: confuses display with the presence of an argument, and raw data can carry an interpretation perfectly well

options.text: Whether the chapter is shorter than the discussion, since a results chapter that runs long has usually begun explaining what the numbers mean
options.misconception: uses length as a symptom, when the symptom appears wherever an interpretation is inserted among the reports

questions.explanation: The division between reporting and interpreting exists so that a reader can check the findings before meeting the account of them. That is a real benefit: a reader who disagrees with a conclusion can look at the report and see exactly what the project found, which is a different and easier dispute to have. It is also the reason a results chapter is often shorter than a student expects, since the work in it is description and the work in a discussion is argument. The division is a matter of where the sentences sit rather than of the vocabulary used, so the second option cannot be right. None of this makes interpretation bad, only early, since a reader who meets a conclusion in the results cannot tell it from a finding.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could disagree with the chapter's conclusions using only the chapter's reports.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Interpretation without overreaching
questions.learningObjective: identify what keeps a discussion chapter within what its results bear
questions.stem: A discussion chapter interprets a project's findings. What distinguishes interpretation from overreach?

options.text: Whether the reading has been kept within what the results can bear, so a rival explanation is offered and weighed rather than assumed away
Whether the chapter restates the results first, since a reader who has the numbers in front of her will judge the interpretation more fairly
options.misconception: names a presentational move, which helps a reader and does not limit the claim the chapter makes

options.text: Whether the wording is cautious, since hedged phrasing is what keeps a conclusion short of the overstatement a confident one produces
options.misconception: treats caution in wording as caution in substance, which a chapter can lose by being quietly hedged throughout

options.text: Whether the chapter engages the other work on the question, since a reading that has not been compared with others has not been tested
options.misconception: makes engagement a guarantee, when a chapter can cite a large literature and still claim more than it has shown

questions.explanation: Overreach is a claim about scope, and the way to avoid it is to ask what else the results would look like if the explanation were wrong. A discussion that names a rival account and says why it is less well fitted to the data has bounded itself honestly, and a reader can now see the boundary. A discussion that assumes the rival away has not bounded itself, and the assumption is usually invisible because it is so widely shared that nobody marks it. The other three options are real features of a good discussion chapter, and each can be present in a chapter that overreaches badly, which is the test of whether it is the distinguishing feature.
questions.hint: Ask what the results would look like if the explanation offered were not the right one.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion that matches the claim
questions.learningObjective: state what a conclusion must claim relative to the body
questions.stem: A conclusion is written after the body of a project is finished. What has to be true for it to do its job?

options.text: That it claims what the body established and no more, since a reader takes a conclusion as the sum of what the work showed
That it is short, since a long conclusion is a reliable sign that the argument was never finished in the body
options.misconception: uses a symptom of a real problem as though the length were itself the defect

options.text: That it repeats the research question in the same words, since a reader needs the question in front of her before the answer can be understood
options.misconception: supplies a presentational requirement, and a conclusion can answer in different words without any loss

options.text: That it proposes further work, since a project which ends by describing its own limits reads as though it were unfinished
options.misconception: treats a stated limitation as a defect, and it is the conclusion that most overreaches when it omits them

questions.explanation: A conclusion is the part of a work that a reader is most likely to quote, and readers quote it without the body, so anything the conclusion claims has to be something the body showed. This is where a project usually loses its own case, since the temptation at the end of two years of work is to state the claim the project would have liked to support. The work is to compare the conclusion with the results, sentence by sentence, and to remove anything that is not there. A conclusion that matches its body is also the more persuasive document, because a reader who has been shown an argument the conclusion keeps faith with has a reason to trust both.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything in the conclusion could be quoted without its evidence and still be fair.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An abstract that matches the body
questions.learningObjective: state the constraint an abstract must satisfy relative to the work
questions.stem: An abstract is often the only part of a paper that a reader will see. What must be true of it?

options.text: That every claim it makes appears in the body, since a summary that outruns its own text misleads precisely the readers who cannot check it
That it is short, since a length limit is what forces a writer to identify the single claim the paper is making
options.misconception: credits a constraint with a benefit, and a short abstract can be as misleading as a long one

options.text: That it names the method, since a reader cannot sensibly judge a result without knowing how it was produced
options.misconception: makes a mention of the method sufficient, and a method named in a sentence can still hide everything that matters

options.text: That it avoids the field's terms, since an abstract is read by people who work in adjacent fields and will not know the vocabulary
options.misconception: assumes the audience for an abstract, which is in practice the field's own readers

questions.explanation: The abstract is unusual in a piece of writing, because it is a part of the work that is read by people who have not read the work. A claim in the body is surrounded by the evidence for it, and a claim in the abstract is not, so the same sentence carries more risk in the shorter document. The practical discipline is to write the abstract last, and then to check every sentence of it against the body, removing anything the body does not contain. The temptation is strongest with the last sentence, where an abstract reaches for a recommendation or a general significance, and those are the sentences most likely to have no counterpart anywhere in the paper.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader who sees only the abstract will believe, and whether the body would support each of it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An executive summary for a non-specialist reader
questions.learningObjective: identify what is hardest to preserve when writing for a non-specialist
questions.stem: An executive summary is written for a reader who does not work in the field. What is the hardest thing to keep while writing one?

options.text: The chain of reasoning, since a reader outside the field needs the argument to hold together without the background the summary leaves out
The brevity, since a summary for a reader with a full diary is judged by how little of it she has to read
options.misconception: treats length as the difficulty when length is the requirement, and the real problem is what has to be left in

options.text: The terminology, since a field's ordinary words are usually opaque to readers from adjacent fields
options.misconception: locates the problem in vocabulary, and a summary can translate terms without losing the reasoning

options.text: The findings, since a result stated in plain words is no longer the result the study actually produced
options.misconception: asserts that plain statement changes findings, and overlooks that a reader can be given the finding itself in fewer words

questions.explanation: A summary for an outsider can lose almost anything except the reasoning, because the reasoning is what makes the report usable. If a reader knows what was found and not why it counts, she cannot tell whether it applies to her situation. If she knows the reasoning and not the finding, she has nothing to act on. So the writing is a matter of keeping a short chain intact: what was found, how it was found in terms she can follow, what it means for the decision she is making, and what it does not settle. The third option is the most common practical problem and it has a straightforward remedy, which is why it is not the hardest thing.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader will do with the summary, and what she needs in order to do it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Compressing a presentation to a time limit
questions.learningObjective: identify what a fixed presentation time forces a presenter to choose
questions.stem: A project must be presented in twelve minutes. What does that limit force on the presenter?

options.text: Choosing what the audience will be able to follow, since a limit of that kind makes depth impossible and leaves only the shape of the argument
Leaving the method undescribed, since a method cannot be explained properly in the time and a bad explanation is worse than none
options.misconception: picks out one section to sacrifice and leaves the question of what the remaining time is for unanswered

options.text: Rehearsing until the timing is secure, since a fixed time rewards a prepared presenter and penalises one who has not practised
options.misconception: gives advice about delivery, which helps and is not the choice the limit forces

options.text: Speaking faster, since both the amount to be said and the time available are fixed and the only free variable is the rate of delivery
options.misconception: assumes the content is fixed when the limit is precisely an instruction to reduce it

questions.explanation: A hard time limit is an instruction about content, and the reason is that a talk has two dimensions and a room can only attend to one at a time. Twelve minutes buys roughly a handful of claims at a rate a listener can follow, and everything beyond that is delivered while the audience is still working on what it has already heard. The decision a presenter has to make is therefore which of the project's claims the audience needs in order to understand the rest, and that is not a decision about method sections or about rehearsal. The fourth option is worth dismissing quickly: speaking faster raises the number of words and lowers the number of ideas the room can hold, so it produces less, not more.
questions.hint: Ask what a listener will have understood by the end, and how many claims that is.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A poster and its reading distance
questions.learningObjective: identify what a poster's reading distance determines
questions.stem: A poster is read by people walking past it at two or three metres. What does that distance set?

options.text: How much the poster can carry, since anything that needs close reading cannot be presented to a reader who is passing at that distance
The type size, since legibility is in the first instance a question of how large a letter must be to be made out across a room
options.misconception: names one consequence of the distance and treats it as the whole of what the distance sets

options.text: The colour scheme, since a reader at that distance will see blocks of colour long before any words can be read
options.misconception: a real and useful design consideration that does not account for the content decisions the distance forces

options.text: How the layout is balanced, since a poster whose visual weight is uneven is harder to take in while somebody is walking past it
options.misconception: concerns the poster's appearance rather than what can be put on it

questions.explanation: Reading distance is a budget of attention and it constrains content before it constrains typography. A reader at three metres can take in a headline, a diagram with one point on it, and a single number, and that is roughly the ceiling. Everything a poster project wants to include, including the method, the sample, the caveats, and the four ways of reading the results, competes for a space measured in glances, and the writer has to decide which of those the poster will do. The other options are all things the distance affects and none of them is the binding one, since a poster with a legible type size and an unreadable amount of content on it has failed.
questions.hint: Ask how long a passer-by will stand in front of the poster, and what can be taken in that time.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The audience a conference panel faces
questions.learningObjective: identify what is different about presenting within a panel
questions.stem: A project is presented on a panel with three others. What is different from a paper given by one person?

options.text: The audience is comparing as well as following, so each talk is being weighed against the others while it is still being given
The time allowed is shorter, since a panel slot gives a presenter less time than a single paper gives its author
options.misconception: a practical difference that is a matter of the session's format rather than of the audience

options.text: The subject matter is narrower, since panels are usually organised around one theme while single papers are offered across a whole field
options.misconception: describes how sessions are arranged rather than what the room is doing while a talk is given

options.text: The questions are harder, since a panel invites questioning from the floor in a way a single paper read to the room does not
options.misconception: a real difference in format, and one that helps rather than the thing the panel changes about the talk

questions.explanation: A panel puts four projects in front of one audience at once, so the audience is doing two things simultaneously. Members are following the talk in front of them and, at the same time, forming a view about how it compares with the others, which is a comparison nobody in the room has the data to make and everybody in the room will make. This changes what a presenter should do. A talk that cannot be placed against the rest, because it gives no sense of what its project assumes the others do, is harder for the room to follow than one that can. The other options describe genuine features of the format, and the first is the one that bears on how the talk should be built.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience is comparing the current talk with while the talk is being given.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The risk of writing for a general audience
questions.learningObjective: identify the risk a non-specialist format adds to a project
questions.stem: A researcher writes a piece about a completed study for readers outside the field. What risk does the format add?

options.text: That the study will be read as a claim about everyone rather than about a sample, since a general reader has no way to supply the limits the study observed
That the study will be misunderstood, since readers outside the field are less likely than specialists to know what the method does
options.misconception: a real difficulty of the format which is a matter of explanation rather than of the claim's reach

options.text: That colleagues will criticise the piece, since writing for a general audience is visible to people whose judgement of the work matters to the researcher
options.misconception: makes the risk a matter of reception among experts, and leaves the content of the claim alone

options.text: That the findings will be exaggerated, since general writing rewards a strong claim more than a careful one
options.misconception: assumes the writer will overstate deliberately, when the usual cause is a format that carries no place for the caveats

questions.explanation: The limits of a study live in its design and its discussion, and a general piece has no room for them, so a reader takes the finding as a statement about the world. A study of four towns becomes a claim about how people choose, and the writer has not made any error of fact, which is what makes the risk difficult to see. The safeguard is structural rather than a matter of care: the piece has to carry its own limits, at least the sample and the setting, in the same register as its findings, so that they cannot be separated. Option four describes the same risk in a form that blames the writer's incentives, and it is the temptation rather than the mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask whether the format has anywhere to put the limits of the study.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A contribution stated as a topic
questions.learningObjective: identify what a stated aim leaves out of a proposal
questions.stem: A proposal's stated aim reads: 'To study how residents in four towns choose a surgery, and to find out whether distance from the surgery affects the choice.' Which description of that aim is accurate?

options.text: It names a subject and a question rather than a contribution, since the sentence stops at what the project would look at and not at what it would leave known
It states a contribution, since a question about whether distance affects the choice is something the project would settle and the existing work has not
options.misconception: credits the aim with a result, when a question is what the project will answer rather than what it will find

options.text: It overstates the scope, since four towns and one outcome is more than a single project can examine closely enough to support a conclusion
options.misconception: identifies a scope problem the aim does not actually have, since four towns and one outcome is a workable design

options.text: It understates the contribution, since a study of four towns establishes less than a study of every town would and should say how much less
options.misconception: measures the aim by the size of the study rather than by what a study of that size could establish

questions.explanation: The aim describes a subject and asks a question about it, and stops there. What a panel needs from an aim statement is the third thing, which is the finding the project expects to be able to report: that the choice does or does not respond to distance in the way the candidate suggests, and at what points. A candidate who can add that sentence has a contribution, and a panel can then ask whether it is already established. Notice that the aim is not wrong and is not vague. It is a perfectly good research plan, and it is silent about the thing the proposal is being judged on, which is the most common defect in this section and the easiest to repair.
questions.hint: Ask what would be known about the choice of surgery after the project that is not known now.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A scope that cannot be examined
questions.learningObjective: identify the cost of a scope a project cannot examine closely
questions.stem: A proposal sets out to examine how one policy changed access to a service nationally over thirty years, in health, education, and housing, and to draw conclusions about the state's overall approach. What is the main risk?

options.text: That the breadth leaves no part examined closely enough to bear a conclusion, since the attention available is the same whether the project looks at three sectors or one
That the necessary records will not exist, since a national account of three sectors across thirty years is unlikely to have been kept in one comparable form
options.misconception: supplies a practical obstacle the candidate could plan around, and it is downstream of the scope choice

options.text: That the findings will be hard to place, since work crossing three sectors belongs to no single literature and so has no obvious readership
options.misconception: concerns where the work could be published rather than what the work would show

options.text: That the conclusion will be unfalsifiable, since a claim about a state's overall approach cannot be checked against any observation
options.misconception: turns breadth into vagueness, when the stated conclusion is a claim about an approach and could be argued against

questions.explanation: The proposal asks for a conclusion about an approach and pays for it with three sectors and thirty years, and the design section is where the arithmetic has to work. To draw a conclusion about a national approach, a researcher has to say what counts as an instance of the policy in each sector, which amounts to a method, and then say what the observed pattern supports. Nothing in the proposal does that, and a panel should treat the absence as the answer to the question. The other three are survivable problems, and each is downstream: a narrower design would reduce the difficulty of the records, the placement of the work, and the vagueness of the conclusion at the same time.
questions.hint: Ask what would count as an instance of the policy in the housing sector, and whether the proposal says.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A methods section that defers everything
questions.learningObjective: identify the defect in a methods section that names stages without specifying work
questions.stem: A proposal's methods section reads: 'Data will be gathered, analysed, and used to test the hypothesis. Instruments and sampling will follow standard practice for this kind of work.' What is missing?

options.text: The particulars a reader would need in order to repeat the study, since naming the stages and deferring to standard practice leaves the work itself unspecified
The name of the instrument, since standard practice in a field amounts to one agreed tool and the proposal has not said which it is using
options.misconception: assumes a single standard instrument is what the reference to practice means, and settles the whole section on one omission

options.text: A sample size, since no analysis can be planned in advance without knowing how many observations the design will produce
options.misconception: picks out one missing particular and presents it as the analysis of the section

options.text: The analysis technique, since the section promises to analyse the data and never says how, which is the most serious omission of the four
options.misconception: singles out one stage as the worst gap, while the section is unspecific at every stage it names

questions.explanation: The section names three stages and specifies none of them, and the phrase about standard practice is what makes that look acceptable. It is a way of appealing to a practice the reader cannot inspect, and a reader who accepted it would be accepting the researcher's account of what the field does rather than the researcher's own design. Notice that every one of the four answers names something genuinely absent, and the reason three of them are wrong is the level at which they operate. A panel is not looking for a sample size. It is looking for a design, and a section that could have been written before the researcher decided anything has not supplied one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the researcher could have written this section before deciding what to measure.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A timeline with no dependencies
questions.learningObjective: read a schedule for the dependency information it fails to carry
questions.stem: A timeline lists six tasks with dates: design the instrument in months one and two, collect responses in months three to five, analyse in months six and seven, write up in months eight and nine. Only the first task has a named owner. What does the timeline fail to show?

options.text: Which tasks depend on which, so a delay to the instrument leaves the collection and the analysis unable to move without anyone seeing the whole chain shift
Whether the nine months are achievable, since a list of tasks that does not show its sequences cannot be added up to a total
options.misconception: makes the schedule unusable as a calculation, when the dates themselves can be added up

options.text: Who is responsible for the tasks after the first, since ownership has been given for the instrument and left off for everything that follows it
options.misconception: catches something the timeline does show as a gap, and treats it as the main thing a schedule must carry

options.text: What the group will do if a task runs late, since a dated list of tasks offers no contingency for a slippage it can plainly foresee
options.misconception: asks for a risk plan, which a proposal schedule does not owe and a dependency chart would not in fact supply

questions.explanation: The dates say when the researcher intends each task to happen, and a plan also has to say what each task is waiting for, and this one does not. The consequence is not a hard calculation, since the months add up perfectly well. It is that the first thing to go wrong cannot be absorbed. If the instrument slips by a month, nothing in the schedule shows that the collection cannot start in month three, and the researcher may discover in month five that the responses are still being designed. A schedule with dependencies on it is also a monitoring tool, since a slipped task shows up as pressure on everything downstream rather than as a single date that has passed.
questions.hint: Ask what happens in month three if the instrument is not ready, and whether the schedule shows it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A significance claim that names a subject
questions.learningObjective: identify what a significance section leaves out of its claim
questions.stem: A proposal's significance section reads: 'This project addresses a topic of considerable importance which, despite that importance, has received comparatively little attention. Work on it is therefore needed.' What is the defect?

options.text: It establishes that the topic matters and that little has been done, and never says what would be known afterwards, so no contribution is claimed at all
It understates the project, since a claim of significance ought to promise a large effect rather than the modest addition this section implies
options.misconception: treats the weakness as a matter of pitch, when the section has not made a claim of any size to pitch

options.text: It argues about the literature rather than about the world, which is the wrong object for a claim about why the work matters
options.misconception: prescribes what a significance claim must be about, and overlooks that attention and importance are the two warrants actually used

options.text: It rests on counting studies, since attention is measured by how many papers exist rather than by what any of them show
options.misconception: identifies a measure the section does not describe, and so locates the fault in a practice it does not use

questions.explanation: Two claims are made here, that the topic is important and that little has been written on it, and both may well be true. Neither is a claim about knowledge, so a panel reading the section still cannot tell what the project would add, and a project that added nothing could have written the same paragraph. The repair is one sentence, and the test of it is whether it could be quoted back as the reason the project was funded. Worth adding that the two warrants in the paragraph are not equally good, since importance is a property the subject already had before the project, whereas a thinness in the literature is at least a fact about the field that somebody can check.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could repeat afterwards as the reason the project was worth funding.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A gap that may be a search error
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a claimed literature gap by examining the search that produced it
questions.stem: A candidate reports that no previous work studies how small charities report their finances, after searching one database using the terms charity and finance. What is the likeliest explanation?

options.text: The terms were the candidate's own, and work that approached the same reporting question from an accounting or a regulatory direction would have been filed under other words entirely
The question really is untouched, since one database and a pair of terms is a reasonable sample of what a field has produced so far
options.misconception: accepts one narrow search as a survey of a literature, and reasons from the absence found to the absence existing

options.text: The work exists but is unpublished, since a question with nothing published about it must be one somebody is still working on
options.misconception: infers a publication status from a search result, which gives no information about what has or has not been written

options.text: The database is itself incomplete, since no single database can be expected to hold the whole output of any field
options.misconception: locates the failure in the source rather than in the query and so leaves the search as run unexamined

questions.explanation: The terms are the candidate's own description of the project, and a search built from them can only find work that describes the problem the same way. Small charities' financial reporting is exactly the kind of question that an accounting researcher and a regulator would both have written about, and both would have filed it elsewhere. This is the most frequent explanation for an apparently striking gap, and the repair is quick: take the terms from the three or four nearest pieces of work the candidate did find and search those, and ask colleagues what they would have called the question. A candidate who does this usually discovers a literature, and a real gap afterwards is far more likely to be the real thing.
questions.hint: Ask what words the nearest existing work would have used for the same reporting question.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A sample that answers a different question
questions.learningObjective: identify the mismatch between a research question and the respondents a plan reaches
questions.stem: A research question asks what teachers think a proposed assessment standard should require. The plan is to survey teachers who have used the standard for at least two years. What is the difficulty with the design?

options.text: Only committed, long-serving teachers are surveyed, so the answers describe people already shaped by the standard rather than the view of the profession that will work under it
The survey will be too small, since views about a standard vary widely and a small sample will not show the range of them
options.misconception: makes the problem one of precision, when the respondents are the wrong people and precision would only make the answer more exact

options.text: The responses will not be reliable, since teachers have an interest in how a standard they must work under is judged
options.misconception: raises a real threat to the responses and leaves the composition of the sample untouched

options.text: The standard will be revised first, since a proposed standard may change before anybody has used it long enough to qualify for the sample
options.misconception: raises a practical difficulty about the timing of the study rather than about who it asks

questions.explanation: The eligibility rule is doing a great deal of work and it is selecting for the wrong people. Two years of using a standard is a long time, and the teachers who have done it are precisely the ones whose views the standard was written for, which means the study will report back a substantial agreement that is an artefact of who was asked. A researcher who wants the profession's view needs the teachers for whom the standard is still unfamiliar, and those are also the harder people to reach, which is why the plan drifted. The fix is to sample across years of experience and to report the two groups separately, so that the difference is visible rather than averaged away.
questions.hint: Ask who the two-year rule selects for, and whose views the question was meant to capture.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion that outruns its finding
questions.learningObjective: identify the unevidenced step in a conclusion drawn from a count
questions.stem: A study reports that teams given a written agenda at the start of a meeting produced a larger number of distinct suggestions, and concludes that agendas improve group deliberation. What has the conclusion left out?

options.text: A route from writing an agenda to deliberating better, since the result is equally consistent with an agenda prompting people who would have stayed silent to speak at all
A larger sample, since a difference in a count of suggestions is a small difference to be confident about on the basis of a few teams
options.misconception: answers a question about precision, while the issue is which of two explanations of the same count the design could separate

options.text: A second kind of team, since one sort of team was studied and the conclusion has been offered about groups of every kind
options.misconception: raises a fair point about reach and presents it as though it were the gap in the explanation

options.text: A judgement of the suggestions themselves, since the study counted ideas and never assessed whether any of the ideas was good
options.misconception: proposes an extra measure, where the deeper problem is that the measure taken does not bear on the claim made

questions.explanation: More suggestions is a fact about quantity, and the conclusion is a claim about quality of thinking, and the design does not connect the two. An agenda could raise the count by improving the deliberation, and it could raise the count by simply calling on people who had not been going to speak, and those two accounts of the same number are indistinguishable in what was recorded. The honest versions of options three and four are both on the table, since a reader would also want to know how far the result reaches and something about the quality of what was produced. The remedy is a design change, or a narrower claim, and in a report already written the second is the only one available.
questions.hint: Ask what else a written agenda could do to the number of suggestions, and whether the design can tell the accounts apart.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An abstract that outruns the body
questions.learningObjective: identify how an abstract can claim more than the work supports
questions.stem: A paper's abstract states that the study shows remote meetings improve team performance by a third and recommends that organisations adopt them. The body reports one team over six weeks, with performance rated by the team's own members, and the discussion lists several reasons the design cannot support a causal claim. Which description is accurate?

options.text: The abstract makes a general causal claim and a recommendation that the body disclaims, so a reader who takes the abstract at its word would act on something the study did not establish
The abstract is accurate and the discussion is overstated, since a section written at the end of a project commonly reaches further than the study itself warrants
options.misconception: assumes the abstract is the faithful section, and reverses which of the two the body contradicts

options.text: The abstract is acceptable, since an abstract states conclusions rather than findings and a stronger claim is conventional in that section
options.misconception: invents a convention under which an abstract may claim what the paper cannot

options.text: The body is at fault for describing a design that cannot support its own conclusion, since the abstract was only reporting what the paper had concluded
options.misconception: assumes the abstract followed the body rather than exceeding it

questions.explanation: The two sections are not describing the same study. The abstract makes a general claim with a quantity in it and draws an organisational recommendation from it, and the body reports a single team, a self-assessment, six weeks, and an explicit statement that the design cannot get at causation. The abstract is the more misleading document precisely because it is the one most readers will see, and because its claim is the kind that leads to a decision. The repair is mechanical rather than intellectual: write the abstract last, extract its sentences, and require a reader to find each one somewhere in the body before it stays.
questions.hint: Ask whether the paper contains a study capable of producing the abstract's claim, and where it is.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The weight of a reviewer's objection
questions.learningObjective: identify what a reviewer's report treats as decisive
questions.stem: A report on a proposal reads: 'The question is important, the reading is well chosen, and the writing is clear. The method, however, cannot distinguish the two explanations the project wants to separate, and the design shows no way of doing so.' How should a candidate read it?

options.text: As a statement that the project as designed cannot answer its own question, which matters more than the praise and the polish would suggest
As a balanced report, since a reviewer who praises the presentation and criticises the method has found a middle position and expects a fix to the method alone
options.misconception: reads balance into a report in which the praise establishes that the objection is about the design

options.text: As a comment on how the proposal reads, since the reviewer has addressed the writing and not what the project would establish
options.misconception: takes the praise as the subject of the report, while the objection is about the project's capacity to answer its question

options.text: As a fixable objection, since an objection about design is the sort a candidate can meet by adding a control condition to the design
options.misconception: assumes a remedy the review has not proposed, when nothing in the report says what would make the design adequate

questions.explanation: The structure of the report is what carries the weight. Everything before the objection establishes that the question, the reading, and the writing are not in question, which means the reviewer found exactly one serious fault and went looking for a long time before finding it. A candidate who reads the first part and stops has been told that a good project is proposed and will be defeated by the design. This is also the report that is easiest to misjudge, because praise feels like a verdict, and it is worth noticing what a report of this kind does not say, which is what design would be adequate, so the candidate's next step is to work that out rather than to reply.
questions.hint: Ask what the praise establishes, and therefore which single thing the report is about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a revise-and-resubmit decision signals
questions.learningObjective: read a revise-and-resubmit decision for what it establishes and withholds
questions.stem: A decision letter reads: 'We would welcome a revised version. The reviewers agree the question matters and the reading is adequate, but the analysis as proposed cannot separate the two candidate explanations. The board makes no recommendation on this submission.' What does the letter say?

options.text: That the fault lies in the design rather than the question, so revision could make the project viable, and the absence of a recommendation is not itself a positive verdict
That the board finds the project promising, since a request for a revision is a form of endorsement and the flat wording is a courtesy
options.misconception: reads a request to see more as praise of what exists, and treats the withheld recommendation as a formality

options.text: That the project is beyond revision, since a board which declines to recommend has concluded that nothing in the design could be changed
options.misconception: infers finality from a withheld recommendation, where the letter in fact asks for a revision

options.text: That the reviewers disagree, since a letter that reports their agreement and then records no recommendation must be describing a split
options.misconception: invents a division the letter explicitly denies by reporting agreement

questions.explanation: The letter has done two things a candidate should separate. It has located the fault, which is a design that cannot separate two explanations the project wants to tell apart, and that is a specific, answerable, and in principle fixable complaint. And it has withheld a recommendation, which is not the same as a negative one, since a board that had concluded the project was hopeless would not have invited a revision. What the letter does not do is endorse, and the candidate who reads it as encouragement will be disappointed. The useful next step is the one the letter implies: work out what design would separate the two explanations, and say in the revision what that design is and why it works.
questions.hint: Ask what the letter identifies as the fault, and what a board with no doubts about the project would have written.
