questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a viva voce question probes
questions.learningObjective: identify what an examiner's question at a defence is testing
questions.stem: A candidate argues that the project's main interview question elicits how participants understood a policy. An examiner asks: 'What would count as an answer from a participant that would show they had not understood it?' What is the examiner doing?

options.text: Asking what would count against the candidate's account, so the question tests whether the design could distinguish understanding from the appearance of understanding
Asking about the wording of the interview guide, since a badly phrased question produces answers that cannot be read as anything
options.misconception: takes a question about validity as a question about wording

options.text: Asking for a second research question, since a design that can be attacked on this point is likely to be attacked on others and the candidate should have a second line ready
options.misconception: treats a challenge to the instrument as a demand for a different project

options.text: Asking about the number of participants, since a study of understanding needs more respondents than a study of preference does
options.misconception: supplies a question the examiner did not ask, and a different kind of defect from the one being probed

questions.explanation: A defence examines the gap between what a candidate claims and what a candidate can show, and this is the standard form that gap takes in qualitative work. The question asks for a negative instance, which is the sharpest form of the probe, because a candidate who can say what would have indicated non-understanding has to have decided what understanding would look like in the data, and a candidate who cannot has been reading coherence into answers. It is a fair question and it is answerable, and the best answers specify the feature of a response that would signal it, together with how the analysis would treat such a case. The other options each substitute a different, easier question.
questions.hint: Ask what the candidate would have to have decided in advance in order to answer the examiner's question.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A response that answers a different question
questions.learningObjective: identify when a reply to a challenge has changed the subject
questions.stem: An examiner asks: 'Your analysis shows the effect before the policy took effect. How do you explain that?' The candidate replies: 'The sample is nationally representative, drawn from four regions, with a response rate above sixty per cent, so the results should be generalisable.' What has the candidate done?

options.text: Answered a different question, since the examiner asked about a timing problem and the reply established something about the sample
Answered what was asked, since a timing problem is a threat to the design and the reply defends the design's most important property
options.misconception: conflates generalisability with the timing of the effect, which are independent properties of a study

options.text: Conceded the point, since describing the sample in detail in answer to a difficulty is a tacit admission that the difficulty stands
options.misconception: reads a change of subject as a surrender, which the reply does not do

options.text: Refused the question, since a candidate who cannot explain an anomaly ought to say so rather than talk about the design instead
options.misconception: labels the reply as evasion, when the candidate has answered a question that was not the one asked

questions.explanation: The examiner's question is about an anomaly in the timing of the effect, and a candidate who cannot explain it may still have a perfectly generalisable sample and a perfectly good response rate. Those two things are independent, and a reply that establishes one while the other is in doubt is answering a different question. The reason this is a common and serious failure at a defence is that reporting the design is the one thing a nervous candidate can do fluently, and the fluency is mistaken for an answer. The repair is to restate the question, answer it, and then add anything about the sample that bears on it, in that order.
questions.hint: Ask whether generalisability would explain an effect appearing before the policy began.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A rigour claim the methods contradict
questions.learningObjective: identify a project's characterisation that its own methods section disconfirms
questions.stem: A report describes its study as methodologically rigorous, with all procedures pre-registered and data collection fully documented in advance. Its methods chapter states that the survey instrument was drafted after the pilot and that the final wording of each item was chosen on the basis of which items produced clearer answers. Which description is right?

options.text: The rigour claim is contradicted by the methods, since a choice made after the pilot cannot have been registered or documented in advance of it
The two are compatible, since a pilot is exactly what registration in advance is meant to account for and the changes made were a consequence of it
options.misconception: reconciles the two by treating a pilot as prior registration, which it is not

options.text: The methods chapter is the one at fault, since a report's opening characterisation takes precedence over a chapter written under time pressure
options.misconception: settles a conflict between two claims by rank rather than by checking what either of them entails

options.text: The claim is about documentation rather than about design, so a choice made after the pilot is still a documented choice and the rigour claim stands
options.misconception: reduces rigour to the existence of records, which is the confusion the claim was making in the first place

questions.explanation: A claim about rigour is a claim about the order in which things were decided, and the methods chapter states an order that contradicts it. Items were written, piloted, and then rewritten in light of how the pilot went, and that is an ordinary and defensible thing to have done. What cannot be true is that the final wording was registered and documented in advance of the pilot, because it did not exist to be registered. The report is not dishonest, and the fix is a characterisation the methods can support: the instrument was piloted, the changes made after the pilot are reported, and the reasons for each change are given. That is a real methodological strength, and it is a much better one to claim.
questions.hint: Ask whether the final wording existed at the moment the report says it was documented.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a contribution claims
questions.learningObjective: state what a contribution claims and what a proposal must add to a topic
questions.stem: A candidate must state a project's contribution rather than its topic. First say what a contribution claims, then say what has to be added to a topic to produce one. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: A claim about what will be known afterwards, since a topic names what will be looked at and a contribution names what the looking yields
A hypothesis to be tested, since a project which states no proposition cannot be said to have addressed anything at all
options.misconception: makes a hypothesis the contribution, while a hypothesis is an input the design tests

options.text: A statement of the method, since a method chosen carefully is a contribution in its own right to a field's practice
options.misconception: credits a method with being a result, which is what makes contributions to a field's practice rare

options.text: An estimate of the project's effect on the world, since a contribution has to be large enough to matter to somebody outside the discipline
options.misconception: sets a size condition on a contribution, and a small reliable result is still a result

questions.explanation: The first answer has to be about knowledge, because that is what a contribution is a contribution to. The second follows from it, and it is a question with a concrete answer: the topic has to be given a claim that somebody could be wrong about, that the existing work does not already establish, and that the design could in principle deliver. A candidate who can write that sentence has a contribution, and a panel can then ask whether somebody else has already delivered it. The other options describe real things a proposal must contain and none of them is the contribution, which is why proposals routinely include all three of them and still fail on this point.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could repeat afterwards and be wrong about.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Establishing that a literature gap exists
questions.learningObjective: state how a gap must be demonstrated and what checking it requires
questions.stem: A candidate claims no previous work addresses their question. First say how the claim was established, then say what would count as checking it. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: How the search was run, since a gap is an absence and the only thing anybody can inspect is the search which failed to find one
How much reading the candidate has done, since the breadth of a search is a fair measure of whether an absence is real
options.misconception: uses effort as evidence, which is the one thing that cannot establish an absence

options.text: Which databases were consulted, since a claim of absence is only as good as the coverage of the places searched
options.misconception: names a necessary part of the account and treats it as a sufficient one, and coverage was never the failure in most such claims

options.text: How long ago the work was done, since an absence across the last ten years is a more interesting gap than an absence across all time
options.misconception: asks about recency, which bears on the value of a gap rather than on whether it exists

questions.explanation: The first answer has to be about the search rather than the conclusion, because a gap is the one claim in a proposal that cannot be evidenced by producing an instance of it. What can be inspected is the procedure: which sources, which terms, which years, which neighbouring literatures, and which combinations of terms were tried. The second answer then says what a check is, which is somebody else re-running that procedure with different vocabulary and arriving at the same absence. The third option is part of the account and worth having, but coverage has been the least of most candidates' problems. The usual failure is the vocabulary, and a candidate who reports the terms they used has shown a reader exactly where to look for the work they missed.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could re-run in order to look for the same absence.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a feasibility claim assumes
questions.learningObjective: identify the prediction a feasibility claim makes and what could break it
questions.stem: A proposal states that the project is feasible. First say what such a claim is predicting, then say what could make it false. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: That the conditions the project depends on will hold, since feasibility is a prediction and a prediction has to name what it is betting on
That the researcher will work hard enough, since feasibility in the end is a matter of the candidate's diligence
options.misconception: locates the prediction inside the researcher, and diligence is not one of the things the claim rests on

options.text: That the budget covers the costs, since feasibility is largely an accounting question about what a project will require
options.misconception: makes cost the whole of feasibility, and omits access and timing which no budget secures

options.text: That the question is answerable at all, since a question nobody can answer makes a project infeasible whatever its resources
options.misconception: conflates worth with feasibility, and the two are the separate questions a panel asks

questions.explanation: A feasibility claim is a prediction, and the first answer has to say what the prediction is about, which is the conditions the project depends on. The second then has a clear job: name the conditions that are outside the researcher's control, since those are the ones that can fail. Access granted by an institution, cooperation from a group, a dataset that is maintained, a window in an academic year, a key person's availability, and in a small project a person staying employed, are all ordinary feasibility conditions and all outside the researcher's gift. A candidate who has listed them has done something useful, because a panel can then weigh a stated risk against a project rather than a promise.
questions.hint: Ask which of the conditions the project needs the researcher cannot promise.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What the data must be able to separate
questions.learningObjective: state what must be distinguished before a design can identify a parameter
questions.stem: A project cannot estimate a parameter from the data it proposes to collect. First say what the data would have to separate, then say what else in those data could move with it. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: Which two things the design has to tell apart, since a parameter that travels with something unmeasured cannot be estimated from these data at any sample size
How large the effect is expected to be, since an effect too small to detect cannot be estimated from a study of any size
options.misconception: makes the problem one of power, when the design cannot separate the explanations whatever the effect size

options.text: How the parameter will be measured, since a quantity with no reliable measure cannot be estimated from a sample at all
options.misconception: raises measurement as though it were the identification problem, which survives perfect measurement

options.text: How many observations the study will collect, since an estimate needs a sample before anything can be said about its precision
options.misconception: supplies the wrong answer to a question the situation has already settled, since more data would not help

questions.explanation: The first answer has to name a pair, because identification is always a matter of telling two things apart. Here it is the part of the pay difference caused by the training and the part caused by everything else that the people who took the training differ on, and the design has to make those two vary independently. The second answer then asks what else could be travelling with the training, and the answer is whatever separates the people who took it from the people who did not. The remaining options all address precision, and they are worth distinguishing because the symptom looks the same from the outside: a project that cannot identify a parameter reports an estimate with a confidence interval around it, and a reader who checks the design will find the interval is about the wrong quantity.
questions.hint: Ask what the project is trying to separate from the training, and what else the people who took it differ on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a methods chapter owes a reader
questions.learningObjective: state what a methods chapter must supply and what it is for
questions.stem: A methods chapter is being written for a final report. First say what a reader would need in order to repeat the work, then say what the chapter is for. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: Every step and every material in enough detail to proceed, since the chapter exists so that somebody else can do the work rather than read about it
The main decisions only, since a chapter that tried to give everything would be unreadable and the details belong in an appendix
options.misconception: assumes a chapter can be complete by being selective, and leaves the reader unable to act on the selection

options.text: The results, since a reader who is going to repeat the work will want to know what the study found before deciding whether to repeat it
options.misconception: puts the findings inside the methods, which is the division the chapter is meant to make possible

options.text: An account of the researcher's reasoning, since a reader cannot evaluate a choice without knowing why it was made that way
options.misconception: requires justification for every choice, and mistakes this for the reporting of them

questions.explanation: The first answer is a practical test applied to every sentence, and it usually settles the argument about a methods chapter in a few minutes. Could somebody else do this? Not would it be reasonable, but could they, without asking the researcher a question? The second answer then says what the chapter is for, which is to be the sufficient instruction for the work and not a defence of it. The fourth option is the interesting one, because justification does belong somewhere in a report, usually in the discussion, where it can be assessed against the evidence. A methods chapter that argues for its own choices gives a reader a reason to distrust them.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could carry out the work from the chapter without asking the researcher anything.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An examiner's challenge to a contribution
questions.learningObjective: identify what a challenge to a contribution is testing and what a reply must do
questions.stem: An examiner tells a candidate that the contribution is smaller than claimed, because the same result has already been reported in a neighbouring field. First say what the challenge is testing, then say what a reply must do. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: Whether the contribution survives being distinguished from the neighbouring result, since a claim of novelty is only as good as what it has been separated from
Whether the neighbouring work was read, since a candidate who has not read a result cannot fairly be told it already exists
options.misconception: makes the challenge about the candidate's reading rather than about the standing of the claim

options.text: Whether the result replicates in a second setting, since a result that holds once is not yet a contribution to anything
options.misconception: sets a standard the candidate's own study may not have been designed to meet

options.text: Whether the two fields describe the same thing, since a difference in vocabulary may be all that separates the two results
options.misconception: makes the challenge a question about terminology, which is one possible answer rather than the test

questions.explanation: The first answer identifies what is really at issue, which is the difference between the candidate's result and the one already reported. Two results can be identical in what they show and different in what they establish, and the difference is usually something about the setting, the population, the mechanism, or what else the result rules out, and a candidate who can state that difference has answered the challenge. The second answer follows, and it is a bounded task: say precisely what the two results share and what only this one shows. The fourth option is worth keeping in mind as a first line of enquiry and is not the whole answer, since a vocabulary difference that resolves in the candidate's favour answers the challenge and a vocabulary difference that does not has to be conceded.
questions.hint: Ask what the new result rules out that the neighbouring one could not, and whether the candidate can say.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A response that concedes too much
questions.learningObjective: identify what an over-generous concession gives up and what it leaves
questions.stem: A candidate is told the study's sample is too narrow for the claim, and replies: 'You are quite right, the sample is narrow, the design has serious limitations, and really the conclusions should not be drawn at all.' First say what the response gives up, then say what a defensible reply would keep. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: The claim as it was stated, since a reply that withdraws the whole conclusion to avoid one objection gives away the part of it that was sound
The candidate's standing with the examiners, since a candidate who agrees too readily gives a panel a reason to doubt the rest of what has been said
options.misconception: describes a reputational cost, while the loss here is to the argument itself

options.text: The findings, since the data were collected and remain the same whatever the candidate says about them at the end
options.misconception: claims a loss to the data, which the reply does not put in question

options.text: The examiner's challenge, since a candidate who accepts a challenge outright deprives the panel of the chance to weigh it against the evidence
options.misconception: describes a loss to the examination rather than to the argument the candidate is making

questions.explanation: The first answer has to be about the claim, and the claim is what has been given away. A sample that is narrow is a limit on how far a result reaches, and it is not a reason that the result is not there, and the difference between those two statements is the difference between a sound project and an absent one. The second answer then says what a defensible reply keeps: the finding, the strength of the evidence for it within that sample, and a claim resized to match, together with the indication of what would be needed to widen it. Candidates concede heavily in defences because the room is looking for honesty, and the honest answer is a narrower claim rather than a withdrawn one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the objection shows the result is not there, or only that it does not reach as far as claimed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a thesis defence examines
questions.learningObjective: state what a defence probes and what a candidate must be able to do
questions.stem: A candidate is examined on a final project. First say what a defence probes, then say what a candidate must be able to do about it. What must the first answer contain?

options.text: The join between the claim and the evidence, since a defence exists to show that the two belong together and not to display the work in general
The candidate's knowledge of the field, since a defence is the last chance to establish that the candidate can operate as a researcher
options.misconception: makes the defence a test of general command of a field rather than of one piece of work

options.text: The completeness of the work, since a project missing a chapter or an analysis has not been finished at all
options.misconception: confuses administrative completeness with the question of whether the argument holds

options.text: The candidate's independence, since a defence establishes that the work was done by the person presenting it
options.misconception: raises authorship, which matters and is not what the examination of the project is for

questions.explanation: A defence is a test of one join, and the join is between what the project claims and what the project shows. The second answer follows: a candidate must be able to state the claim, show where in the work each part of it is evidenced, name the limits of that evidence, and say what would have to be added for the claim to reach further. A candidate who can do that has nothing to fear from a panel, whatever the panel's opinion of the field. questions.topic: Which abstract matches the study
questions.learningObjective: select the abstract that the body of a paper supports
questions.stem: A paper reports a study of a retention initiative introduced for one cohort at one college, comparing retention for that cohort with a cohort that did not have it, and finding a difference of two percentage points, which the design cannot separate from one other difference between the two cohorts. Four abstracts are offered. Which one matches the body?

The study establishes that retention initiatives improve retention, and recommends extending them across the sector
options.misconception: turns a two-point difference the design cannot separate from a rival cause into a general result and a sector-wide recommendation

options.text: The study provides a thorough account of retention initiatives in higher education, drawing on all available data
options.misconception: presents one college and two cohorts as a comprehensive treatment, so a reader would expect far more than the study offers

options.text: Retention fell among the cohort receiving the initiative, which gives cause for concern about the sector's approach
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the finding and adds a worry about a sector, so a reader would act on the opposite of what the study showed

questions.explanation: Only the first abstract is a report of what the study did and found, including the rival explanation the design could not exclude, and a reader who sees only that abstract would not be misled. The second turns a two-point difference it cannot separate from another cause into a general result and a recommendation for a whole sector, which is the commonest form of overreach. The third is a puff piece that a reader would take for a comprehensive treatment, when the work concerns one college and two cohorts. questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Where an interpretation has been placed
questions.learningObjective: identify an interpretation sitting in a results report
questions.stem: A results chapter contains: 'Table 3 shows the two groups did not differ on any measure. The pattern is therefore consistent with no effect, and the reason must be that the instrument is insensitive.' Four descriptions of the chapter follow. Which is right?

options.text: An explanation has been placed inside the report, since the last sentence offers a cause the data cannot support and the report should have stopped at the difference
The results are reported correctly and the explanation belongs in the discussion, which makes this a matter of placement rather than of the evidence
options.misconception: treats the fault as one of placement, while the sentence offers a cause that no set of null comparisons can establish

options.text: The results are under-reported, since a null result should be presented as showing the effect is absent rather than as leaving it open
options.misconception: presses a null result into a claim that the effect is absent, which is a different finding from a design that could not detect a small effect

options.text: The explanation is warranted, since a measure that finds no difference in any of several comparisons is usually a measure of nothing
options.misconception: assumes that finding no difference across several measures shows the measure is broken, and it is one of several explanations on offer

questions.explanation: The first two sentences report, and the third does not. Nothing in a set of null comparisons tells you why they are null, and the instrument's insensitivity is one of several available explanations, among them a real effect cancelled by something, a design that could not detect a small effect, and chance. Placing a guess in the report means a reader has to work out which sentences are findings before they can assess them. Option two is the closest and is worth separating from the answer, because the placement objection and the evidential objection are different, and only the second is decisive: the sentence would be a problem wherever it was put unless the evidence were supplied.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence a reader could not have written down from the data alone.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An executive summary that reaches a non-specialist
questions.learningObjective: select the summary written for a reader outside the field
questions.stem: A study of appointment waiting times reports: patients waited longer; waiting varied more by referral route and by region than by a patient's age; the study used regional administrative records over three years. Four executive summaries are offered for a board of an organisation that commissions appointments. Which is the one written for that reader?

options.text: It gives the finding, gives the comparison that accounts for most of the variation, and recommends publishing waits by route so that patients can choose with the information in front of them
It reports the finding and recommends nothing, on the ground that a summary for an organisation should avoid asking it to act on anything
options.misconception: declines the only part a commissioning reader would use the summary for, and a summary recommending nothing has given away its purpose

options.text: It states that waiting times have increased steadily year on year, which is the conclusion a reader will want from a study of this length
options.misconception: converts a comparison between groups into a trend over time, which three years of records would be needed to support

options.text: It explains that the analysis employed a fixed-effects specification with region and route controls, and reports the principal coefficient
options.misconception: presents a methods section to a reader who cannot evaluate a specification, so the coefficient arrives with nothing to interpret it

questions.explanation: The first summary is the one a board can use, because it says what was found, says which comparison accounts for most of the variation, and draws a recommendation that follows from that comparison rather than from the fact that a study was done. The other three each fail a different way. The second declines the only part a commissioning board would use it for. The third converts a comparison across groups into a trend over time, which three years of records would be needed to support and which the study does not report. The fourth is a methods section, and a reader who cannot evaluate a specification has no way to use the coefficient it produces.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is going to do after reading, and whether the summary enables it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rejection letter leaves open
questions.learningObjective: identify what a rejection is about and what it leaves available
questions.stem: A decision letter reads: 'The board thanks you for the proposal. The question is well posed, but the design cannot address it with the material available, and the board does not see an alternative design within the project's scope. We are not able to proceed with this submission in this cycle.' Four readings follow. Which is right?

options.text: The decision is about the design rather than the question, so the letter closes this submission and leaves a differently designed project open
The decision is final about the whole project, since a board that has declined a submission has declined the work it proposed
options.misconception: reads a decision about one submission as a judgement on the whole project, and the letter makes no such claim

options.text: The decision is a delay, since a board which sees no alternative design now may well see one in a later cycle
options.misconception: treats a possible future cycle as a promise, where the letter offers none

options.text: The decision is a criticism of the question, since praise for a question in a letter is conventionally a way of softening a rejection of it
options.misconception: assumes praise in a decision letter is ironic, when the letter is explicit about where the objection lies

questions.explanation: The letter names what it objected to and what it did not, and the exception is at the end rather than the beginning. It praises the question, faults the design, and says it sees no alternative within the scope, which is a statement about this proposal from this candidate and not about the question. What a candidate should do is take the design objection seriously and ask whether the question can be answered by some means the project has not considered, including some that would make it a different and smaller project. The second and fourth readings both over-read the letter, and the third is a hope rather than a reading: nothing in it promises a future cycle.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the proposal the letter praises and which part it faults, and what follows from that division.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What an appeal can achieve
questions.learningObjective: identify what determines the prospects of an appeal against a decision
questions.stem: A candidate's proposal is rejected, and the letter identifies one design fault. The candidate appeals, on the ground that the board misunderstood the design as described. Four accounts of the appeal follow. Which is right?

options.text: The appeal asks the board to read again what it has read, so its prospects turn on whether the design was in fact described rather than on the strength of the argument made now
The appeal should succeed if the argument is right, since a board which has misunderstood a proposal has made an error the candidate is entitled to have corrected
options.misconception: assumes a correct argument forces a reversal, where the board is being asked to re-read a document it has already read

options.text: The appeal is out of time, since a decision of this kind cannot be appealed once the cycle in which it was made has closed
options.misconception: declares the appeal time-barred without any stated rule about timing, which the account of the appeal does not supply

options.text: The appeal belongs to the reviewers rather than the board, since the reviewers wrote the comments the decision relied upon
options.misconception: redirects the appeal to the reviewers, though the decision being appealed was the board's own

questions.explanation: An appeal against a misunderstanding is the weakest kind there is, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of how it is written. The board is being asked to reverse a decision on the ground that it read the proposal incorrectly, and the only evidence available is the candidate's own account of how it reads. The one thing that can help is a specific passage, quoted, that bears directly on the point the board raised, together with an acknowledgement of whatever in the proposal was genuinely unclear. The second reading is the one candidates want, and it is the one that converts an appeal into a resubmission. A candidate who has a design that would have worked is better off writing a new proposal than arguing about the old one.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence the candidate can offer that the proposal said something other than what the board took it to mean.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The audience a panel makes
questions.learningObjective: identify what a panel audience does while a talk is being given
questions.stem: A presenter has twelve minutes in a four-project panel, in front of a room of specialists and of people who have to act on this work. Four descriptions of the audience follow. Which is right?

options.text: The room is following the talk and weighing it against the other three at the same time, so each project is being compared before any of them has finished
The room is a specialist room, since sessions are organised by a field and the audience follows whoever convened the session
options.misconception: settles the room into one group and so misses the comparison a panel makes the audience do throughout

options.text: The room is a practitioner room, since a panel mixing specialists and practitioners is convened to be useful to the people who will have to act
options.misconception: also fixes the audience as one group, and leaves the comparison between the four projects unexplained

options.text: The room is two rooms, so the presenter should choose one of them and address that one properly rather than splitting the talk
options.misconception: proposes to escape a problem the panel creates for every audience rather than working with it

questions.explanation: The feature that makes a panel different is comparative, and it operates whether or not the room is mixed. Every member of the audience is doing two things, following the current talk and forming an estimate of it against the other three, and the second activity is one nobody has the data to do properly, so it goes on throughout. A talk that does not signal where it stands in relation to the rest gives the room nothing to compare, and the comparisons get made on presentation instead. The other readings each settle the audience into one group or the other, and the fourth offers a way of dealing with a situation the panel creates whether it is addressed to specialists or to practitioners.
questions.hint: Ask what the audience is doing with the other three projects while this one is being given.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Assembling a proposal in order
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of building a proposal so each depends on the one before
questions.stem: A candidate must assemble a research proposal. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: State the question the project will answer, since everything later in the proposal is a way of showing that the question can be answered
Establish what the existing work has not settled, since the question only takes shape once a reader knows what it is answering
Set out the design that would answer it, since a gap becomes an opportunity only when there is something to do about it
Say what would be known afterwards, since a proposal is judged on the knowledge it produces and not on the subject it examines
Give the schedule together with what each task depends on, since a design nobody can sequence is a design a reader will doubt

questions.explanation: The order runs from the thing being asked to the things that make the asking credible, and each step is a precondition for the next. The question first, because without it there is nothing for the rest of the proposal to be about, and it is the step candidates most often take last, when the design has hardened into something the question has to be bent to fit. The gap second, because it is what gives the question its point and it is the step most often taken first, before the question has been understood. The design third, since it has to answer the question as stated. The contribution fourth, because it can only be written once the design is settled. The schedule last, when there is a plan worth sequencing.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done first, would leave the other four with nothing to serve.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequencing the chapters of a long work
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of structuring a long argument
questions.stem: A writer must structure a long piece of work. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: Settle in mind what the work concludes, since the chapters have to be arranged to carry a reader to that conclusion rather than merely to contain it
Decide what each chapter will argue, since a chapter without an argument of its own is a section of the work rather than a part of the case
Order the chapters so that each rests on the one before, since a reader who meets the evidence first has no reason for reading it
Decide where the existing work is discussed, since its place determines which chapters a reader can understand on arrival
Write up the method last, since a design chosen to fit a settled argument is a different design from one chosen before the argument was known

questions.explanation: Structure is decided from the end backwards, which is why the first step is a conclusion the writer may not yet be sure of and has to hold provisionally. The chapter claims come next, and doing them at this stage is what stops a long work turning into a heap: a chapter with no claim of its own is a place to put material rather than a step in an argument. The order of the chapters is then a question of dependence, and it is not the order the material was gathered in. The literature is placed where the reader needs it rather than collected at the front, and the method comes last because it is easier to describe than to defend and because describing it before the claim is settled is how a design ends up fitted to a conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done last, would leave the writer with chapters they cannot order.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Handling a challenge at a defence
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of answering an examiner's challenge
questions.stem: An examiner challenges a candidate's project in a defence. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: Work out what the challenge is testing, since a challenge that has not been understood cannot be answered at all
Say which part of the claim it touches, since a reply that answers every possible objection has conceded something nobody asked for
Put the strongest version of the challenge, since a reply built on a weak version collapses when the examiner presses the strong one
Answer it and say what follows for the claim, since a defence ends with a claim rather than with an exchange of replies
Record what was conceded, since a concession made in the room has to appear in the submitted version or the record and the work will not agree

questions.explanation: The order is defensive in the useful sense, and each step is a precondition for the next. Understanding the challenge first is not a courtesy to the examiner, since most failed defences are answers to a question the candidate guessed at rather than the one asked. Bounding the challenge comes next, because a candidate who answers a broader question than was put has widened the ground on which the claim can be attacked. The strong version is then necessary, because a weak restatement is the version the examiner will abandon, and only when it is pressed will its weakness show. The claim is restated last of all, and it is the last thing said because a defence is judged on what the candidate claims afterwards. The final step is administrative and is the one most often forgotten.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done first, would leave the candidate answering a question the examiner did not ask.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Revising after a revise-and-resubmit decision
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of revising a proposal after a review
questions.stem: A candidate has been invited to revise a proposal. Put the steps in the order that lets each depend on the one before it.

options.text: Identify the defect the reviewers identified, since that is the thing the revised version has to repair and nothing else is worth the effort yet
Check what else depends on the defect, since a change to a design moves the analysis, the schedule, and every claim derived from either
Reply to the reviewers point by point, since a reader of the revision needs to see that each objection was taken seriously rather than ignored
Say what has not changed and why, since a revision that alters something without saying so invites the same objection in the next round
Keep a record of the arguments made and dropped along the way, since a later reader will ask why the design looks the way it does

questions.explanation: The sequence protects the candidate from the commonest failure, which is to rewrite the whole proposal and to leave the defect in it. Locating the defect first keeps the revision proportionate, and checking what depends on the defect comes immediately after, since the reviewers have found something structural and fixing it will move three other parts of the document. The point-by-point reply then has something real to point at, and the statement of what has not changed is what tells a reader the revision was deliberate rather than a fresh draft. The last step is the one that pays off months later, when the reason for a design decision has to be reconstructed and the candidate is no longer available to explain it.
questions.hint: Ask which step, done last, would leave the reviewers unable to tell what was done about their objection.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why a literature gap is hard to verify
questions.learningObjective: explain why a claimed gap resists verification and what a candidate should do about it
questions.stem: Explain why a literature gap is hard to verify, and what a candidate should do when asked to show that one exists.

answer.exemplar: A gap is a claim about an absence, and the ordinary tools for establishing a claim are built for showing that something is there. Quoting a source proves the source exists; running a search that returns nothing proves nothing at all, because a search that returns nothing and a search run badly return the same result. The vocabulary problem makes this worse rather than better, since a candidate searches with the phrase they have for their own question and a literature that approached the same problem from a neighbouring discipline filed it under that discipline's terms, and the work never reaches the results. A second difficulty is the asymmetry of evidence, since finding the missing work is a false negative that teaches the candidate something and finding nothing is a false positive that teaches them nothing, so the only informative searches are the ones that fail. What follows is a practical discipline. Report the search rather than the conclusion: which sources, which terms, which years, which neighbouring literatures, and which combinations were tried, so that a reader can see where it was thin and re-run it. Then take the terms used by the three or four nearest existing studies and search those, ask colleagues what they would have called the question, and search the reference lists of those nearest works, since a review that cites a review is often the shortest route to the literature a candidate believes is absent. And expect the gap to shrink. A gap that survives a search run this way is more likely to be real, and a genuine gap is also more likely to be a question nobody can answer with the data available, which is worth discovering before the project starts rather than after.

questions.explanation: A strong response explains that a gap is an absence and so cannot be evidenced by exhibiting anything, that a null search result is uninformative because a badly run search returns the same, that the usual cause of a spurious gap is the candidate's own vocabulary, and that the searches worth running are the ones likely to fail. It should give the practical repair, which is to report the search rather than the conclusion, borrow the terminology of the nearest work, and check reference lists, and should note that a real gap often signals a question that is hard rather than untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what a search returning nothing can tell you, and what words the nearest existing work would have used.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: How a rigour claim can contradict the methods
questions.learningObjective: explain how a project's characterisation of its own rigour can be disconfirmed by its methods
questions.stem: Explain how a project can describe its own methods as rigorous and be contradicted by what the methods chapter says happened.

answer.exemplar: A characterisation of rigour is a claim about the order in which decisions were made, and an order is exactly what a methods chapter reports, so the two can come apart in a way no amount of good writing repairs. The common case is the pilot. Piloting an instrument is good practice, and choosing after a pilot to keep the items that produced clearer answers, to reword the ones participants stumbled over, and to drop the ones nobody could answer is better practice than freezing an instrument before anyone has used it. A report can then describe itself as having pre-registered its procedures while its own methods chapter records that the final wording of the instrument was settled on the basis of how the pilot went, and the two statements cannot both be true, because at the moment of registration the final wording did not exist. The reason the contradiction is not usually noticed is that the two claims live in different parts of a document and are read for different purposes, the opening characterisation for the impression and the methods chapter only by somebody checking. The repair is to describe what was done rather than to pick a better adjective, and the description here is genuinely strong: the instrument was piloted, the changes made after the pilot are reported, the reason for each change is given, and the number of changes is small. A candidate who swaps the characterisation for that description has a methods section a reader can trust on a specific question, which is worth more than a claim about rigour that the reader has already found to be untrue.

questions.explanation: A strong response identifies that a rigour claim is a claim about the order of decisions and that a methods chapter reports that order, so a contradiction between them is possible and easy to miss because the two statements sit in different parts of a document. It should use the ordinary case of a piloted instrument whose items were revised afterwards, explain that this is good practice, and end by saying the repair is to describe what was done, since a reported pilot with a small number of justified changes is a stronger claim than an unsupported one about rigour.
questions.hint: Ask what the word rigour is a claim about, and whether the methods chapter reports the same thing.
